Based on the representation shown in Figure 1, next, we discuss the common attributes across these designs: • Utility/grid: These data centers are powered by the utility/grid as the primary source of energy. The data centers are typically fed by a medium-voltage (13.8-kv–34.5-kV) supply from a utility substation, which is then stepped down to low-voltage (~400-V) supply for the IT and cooling loads in the data center. • Transfer switches: Depending on the uptime requirements, appropriate redundancies are implemented in the power distribution system feeding the IT and cooling loads. These redundancies facilitate, e.g., concurrent maintainability and automatic failover to an alternate power feed to deliver to the uptime requirements. The presence of the redundancy is managed through appropriate automatic or static transfer switches, as shown in Figure 1 (a), (e). • IT load: Data center IT hardware (e.g., computing servers, network servers, storage servers) are voltage-sensitive equipment, and their power quality requirements are governed by the Information Technology Industry Council (ITIC) curve (Elphick and 5 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Smith 2010). The ITIC curve is published by ITIC (formerly known as the Computer and Business Equipment Manufacturers Association [CBEMA]), and it provides an AC voltage boundary that most IT equipment can tolerate or ride through without experiencing unexpected shutdowns or malfunctions. Figure 2 shows the ITIC curve: It shows that the input AC voltage below 0.7 p.u. is considered a dropout event, and a 1.2- p.u. overvoltage is acceptable for up to 3 milliseconds. The typical IT load is approximately 400 V, so the appropriate transformation of the medium-voltage supply from the substation needs to be incorporated into the design. • UPS: To mitigate AC supply voltage fluctuations outside the allowable region within the ITIC curve, most data center power systems have UPS units. The UPS has batteries and can support the IT load for a few minutes. Figure 2. Most data centers rely on generators (diesel, natural gas, hydrotreated vegetable oil) as a backup energy source (Uptime Institute. n.d) (Figure 1 (a) to (e)), and some newer designs are relying on BESS (Figure 1 (f)). In particular, the generators are to be used only when the utility is not available, and the transition is managed through automatic transfer switches (see Figure 1 (a), (b), (c), (d), (e)). The backup energy source (generators and/or BESS) are connected at a low voltage in some designs (such as in Figure 1 (a), (b), (c), (e)) and at the medium-voltage level in others (Figure 1 (d) and (f)).
